summary: Asks Hosts to warn their users when the local IMP announces it is going down. BBN Report 1822 defines an IMP-to-Host message that says when the IMP will go down, for how long and why, but Hosts were not reliably passing that on to people using the network.

eli5.summary: When the power company says the lights will go off soon, you should tell everyone in the house. This note asks computers to warn their users the same way.

subtitle: Asking hosts to warn users when the local IMP is going down.

tldr.problem: When an IMP (Interface Message Processor) goes down, some hosts received the IMP Going Down message but did not communicate this impending outage to their users, who would be surprised when network connectivity disappeared.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 548 urges all Hosts to display or notify their network users when they receive an IMP Going Down message from the local IMP, rather than only logging the message as many Hosts were doing.
tldr.outcome: Better preparation for planned network maintenance and reduced user frustration during scheduled downtime periods, which were typically scheduled on Tuesday mornings.

today: RFC 548 represents early thinking about operational best practices. While host systems and maintenance scheduling have changed dramatically since 1973, the principle of communicating planned outages to users remains a best practice in modern operations.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content: BBN Report 1822, which specifies how hosts connect to IMPs, defines IMP-to-Host message type 2 as the IMP Going Down message. This message tells the Host that the local IMP is going down, specifies when it will go down, for how long, and why. However, many Hosts receiving this message were only logging it to a teletype rather than actively notifying their users. This meant that network users would be unprepared when their connectivity suddenly disappeared without warning.
sections.eli5: The network hardware warns your computer before it shuts down for maintenance, but your computer wasn't telling the people using it about this planned outage.

sections.title: What Should Happen
sections.content: RFC 548 urges all Hosts to actively warn their network users (both users logging in remotely and local users of network services) when an IMP Going Down message is received. Rather than merely logging the information passively, Hosts should display the message to their users, giving them time to finish work, disconnect gracefully, or make other arrangements. The RFC notes that planned network maintenance occurs every Tuesday morning from 7 a.m. to 9 a.m. Eastern Time, as had been announced in RFC 440.
sections.eli5: Hosts should show a message to all their users saying the network is about to go down, so people know to save their work.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content: When an IMP Going Down message is received but users are not notified, network connectivity will be lost without warning. This can lead to lost work, interrupted computations, and user frustration. By warning users in advance, Host administrators give them time to save their work, gracefully close network connections, and prepare for the outage. This simple practice of communication improves the user experience during scheduled maintenance windows.
sections.eli5: If you do not tell people the network will go down, they might lose their work. A simple warning gives them time to save and prepare.
